item.title: Pope Leo XIV arrives for South American tour after cancer surgery
item.description:
A mototaxi drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV in Chiclayo, Peru, on Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his trip to Latin America. AP Photo/Martin Mejia Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship. As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America. Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. item.title: Several Democrats renew calls for datacenter pauses after blue wave
item.description:
AUSTIN, Texas — As the Democrats’ blue wave began to slam into Texas, Richard Torres, a Texan who has voted blue his entire life, kept peering at the results pouring in on reporters’ screens all around him. And when it was announced Texas state Rep. James Talarico had toppled Ken Paxton, he sat down to take it in. Torres was the former chair of the Williamson County Democratic Party, where Talarico grew up and attended high school in Round Rock, Texas. He never thought that Texas Republicans would be swept away by the oncoming blue wave. item.title: Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison
item.description:
A Kenyan doomsday cult leader was sentenced Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people after ordering followers to starve themselves to meet Jesus. Pastor Paul Mackenzie was sentenced by Kenya’s High Court in the coastal city of Mombasa after being convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult, according to the Associated Press. He received two consecutive 100-year terms: one for murders by starvation and another for murders by direct homicide. Justice Diana Kavedza said Mackenzie, the leader of the Good News International Church, bore the “primary criminal culpability” for leading his followers into an isolated area and directing them to starve themselves to death, the outlet reported. “The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law,” the judge added. item.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Bottoms reflects on historic victory and the path forward for Democrats
item.description:
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms hugs her daughter Lincoln during an election night watch party in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 3, 2026. Megan Varner/Getty Images There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers. Georgia remembers. The auction blocks . The cotton fields . The lynching trees . The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves. And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor . The first Black woman elected governor of any American state. Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia. An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. item.title: What to know about Gina Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect
item.description:
AUSTIN, Texas — Gina Hinojosa is set to become the next governor of Texas after voters denied Republican Gov. Greg Abbott a fourth term, a stunning upset by a state legislator who will become the first Latina to hold the Lone Star State’s top job. Hinojosa mounted a competitive bid against Abbott with a disciplined focus on corruption, which she argued is to blame for soaring prices, declining public schools and the aggressive expansion of data centers. Hinojosa capitalized on the financial strain that pushed voters who had supported President Donald Trump to grow disillusioned with the Republican Party. “It bothered me that they doubted us,” Hinojosa told a crowd of supporters at an election night event in Austin to uproar. “Now I stand before you humbled and grateful.” Hinojosa will be the first Texas governor from the Rio Grande Valley, a heavily Latino part of the state, and the…

item.title: California’s new teen social media law challenged in court by Meta, TikTok and Google
item.description:
In summary California’s ban on addictive social media features for kids takes effect in January. Now Big Tech is trying to stop it in federal court. Tech giants Meta, Google, and TikTok are suing to block a landmark California law meant to protect kids’ mental health on social media platforms. The law, one of a slate of bills signed by Gov. Newsom this year to protect kids online, would block social media companies from offering “addictive” features to teens under 16. Set to go into effect in January, the law defines addictive features as design choices like infinite scroll, autoplay, and recommendations. Those features are blamed in part for a teen mental health crisis, which the law seeks to curb. item.title: Latino voters propel Democrats to big wins with leftward swing
item.description:
AUSTIN — Texas. Florida. Pennsylvania. Colorado. Arizona. Nevada. California. The historic landslide of Latino voters toward Democrats hit battleground after battleground Tuesday, crumbling the coalition that helped carry President Donald Trump to victory just one cycle ago. “This is an earthquake,” Democratic Latino operative Sergio Gonzalez told POLITICO on the sidelines of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s victory party in Austin. “Latinos were angry. They were angry this election.” While the entire country shifted toward Democrats, nowhere shifted as dramatically as predominantly Latino areas. item.title: We’ve just seen a transformative moment in America’s death penalty history | Austin Sarat
item.description:
In summary If approved by the California Supreme Court, the number of people sentenced to death nationwide would drop by nearly a third. California Gov. Gavin Newsom today moved to commute the death sentences of all 548 people facing execution in the state, allowing them to instead serve life sentences without the possibility of parole. The California Supreme Court must approve some of these commutations. If it does, Newsom’s action would be responsible for the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history . “I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he wrote in an open letter to Californians . Newsom’s decision, which his office said would benefit 529 men and 19 women, does not guarantee they will all be resentenced. The justices will have to decide…
